ASSUMPTION: Every critique below is judgment from general baseball-operations structure. None is verified, and no figure is quoted because none was supplied.
ASSUMPTION: The attached assumptions are pooled across many ideas, and many (rain delays, stolen bases, draft pools, ticketing) are irrelevant to these six. Only those matching each IDEA text are used.

ASSUMPTION: [1 Coaching hire] The decision recurs only a few times a year, and each hire is a single, unrepeatable choice. The value at stake is unquantified, and the ledger's sign is unknown.
ASSUMPTION: [1] Public staff data is not point-in-time clean. Titles, assistant and minor-league roles and start dates in press releases and media guides are incomplete and revised after the fact.
ASSUMPTION: [1] Few players move organizations alongside a given coach. Movers are selected (acquired because the club expects improvement) and coach credit is shared among several staff. Playing time, health and the player's own regression to the mean are further confounders.
ASSUMPTION: [1] A retrospective test is possible if ratings built through year T predict player change under the same coach in T+1 better than a tenure-and-reputation proxy. The number of coaches with enough movers may be too small for intervals narrow enough to change a hire.
ASSUMPTION: [1] Outcome observability is weak because the counterfactual is missing. Clubs with private tracking and biomechanics data probably evaluate coaches better than any public panel can.
ASSUMPTION: [1] It would look useful by ranking coaches whose past-year gains are mostly regression to the mean. The ranking would look reasonable with no persistence, so year-over-year persistence is the key falsification test.

ASSUMPTION: [2 Non-tender] This recurs annually with a hard early-December deadline (unverified; the CBA may change it). The value at stake is each eligible player's projected arbitration salary minus replacement cost, which is real but unquantified.
ASSUMPTION: [2] Salary projections are public-ish and available at decision time. The replacement market (who will be non-tendered league-wide, and at what price) is not known when the Cubs decide, so the forecaster must predict other clubs' choices.
ASSUMPTION: [2] A backtest has many player-years, but price and next-season output are observed only for players who signed. Players who retired, went abroad or signed minor-league deals create survivorship bias.
ASSUMPTION: [2] The baseline (tender if WAR per dollar beats a threshold) is the same quantity the forecaster uses, so gains may be only a threshold re-tune. The prior finding that a simple rule captures most of the value in the low-attention pool suggests a ceiling here too.
ASSUMPTION: [2] It would look useful from post-hoc selection of bargain non-tendered players, where single-season WAR noise is large and winners are remembered. Sophisticated clubs already carry internal projection and arbitration models.

ASSUMPTION: [3 Qualifying offer] The decision is annual but applies only to the Cubs' own pending free agents who meet eligibility rules. The Cubs' eligible list is unknown, so expected value may be near zero in many years.
ASSUMPTION: [3] The QO amount, acceptances and signings are public, but the number of cases per year is small. The accepted and declined classes are lopsided, so calibration is weak and one executive's judgment may match it.
ASSUMPTION: [3] The idea's baseline ("offer when market AAV clearly exceeds the QO") already needs a market AAV estimate. The model replaces that estimate, so the claimed edge reduces to forecast accuracy on a handful of players.
ASSUMPTION: [3] The compensation-pick value depends on CBA terms that may change at expiration (unverified). Counterfactual value cannot be observed, and acceptance is driven by player preference, health and agent strategy that public signals miss.
ASSUMPTION: [3] It would look useful through rare, memorable accepted-QO cases and high accuracy on obvious calls such as a star who is declined.

ASSUMPTION: [4 NPB/KBO posting] This is a handful of events per year across the league, and the Cubs only matter when they pursue a given player. Per-signing value is plausibly large but unquantified.
ASSUMPTION: [4] The posting window is largely public. Ownership of NPB pitch-tracking and detailed batted-ball data is limited, and what is public may lag decision time.
ASSUMPTION: [4] Previously posted players with MLB outcomes are few, so the translation model has high variance and heterogeneous eras and league environments. Outcomes are observable but censored, because players who were not signed leave no MLB data.
ASSUMPTION: [4] The winner's curse means a more accurate public model still does not give an edge unless the Cubs bid below the consensus. Clubs with international scouting, video and private data are likely ahead, and the idea overlaps minor-league translation work.
ASSUMPTION: [4] It would look useful by fitting the few posted stars in hindsight, with overfit coefficients and nothing out of sample.

ASSUMPTION: [5 Postseason roster] The decision recurs only in years the Cubs qualify, one to four times a year by the candidate's own text. Expected annual value is discounted by qualification probability (unknown).
ASSUMPTION: [5] Rosters, opposing starters and platoon splits are public at the decision time. Injury status at the roster deadline may be incompletely public.
ASSUMPTION: [5] Pooled league-wide postseason rosters give a modest number of series, but each series outcome is dominated by noise. A series-win-probability difference from the 25th and 26th roster spots may be too small to detect with any realistic sample.
ASSUMPTION: [5] Alternatives are not observed, so the backtest is a simulation scored by its own model and can embed the biases it tests. Clubs likely already run internal series simulators.
ASSUMPTION: [5] It would look useful by retrofitting a few memorable pinch-runner or reliever moments in a winning run, which is outcome bias.

ASSUMPTION: [6 Arbitration filing] This recurs every January across the arbitration-eligible roster, and awards compound into later raises, so it is among the more regular decisions. The value is capped by the gap between the two filed numbers, since the panel picks one.
ASSUMPTION: [6] Filed numbers, results and the comparable-player rules are largely public. The exact arguments and the panel's reasoning are not, and hearings are rare because most cases settle. Settlements are not hearing outcomes, so the training labels come from a selected subset.
ASSUMPTION: [6] The count of historical hearings may be too small and shifts with CBA rule changes (expiration date and new rules unverified). Whether to settle or go to hearing is a strategic choice also tied to club policy and player relations, not just EV.
ASSUMPTION: [6] The baseline (midpoint settlement) is a hearing-free outcome, so the EV comparison needs an assumed hearing probability and a model of player willingness. Specialized staff and outside counsel probably already hold this knowledge.
ASSUMPTION: [6] It would look useful through a predictor tuned to hearing outcomes in which the filing midpoint alone already predicts the winner, and through ignoring that club-won and player-won cases are selected by who chose to go to hearing.

ASSUMPTION: [Blind spot] Dollar and win value at stake is unquantified for all six. Rank the candidates by value times decision count times the maximum plausible edge before building anything.
ASSUMPTION: [Blind spot] Sample size is the shared weakness (QO, posting, postseason, hearings, coach movers). Pooling league-wide raises n but strips Cubs-specific context, and no tool can beat a simple baseline with only a few dozen noisy labels.
ASSUMPTION: [Blind spot] Many of these decisions are driven by counterparties (agents, player preference, rival bidders, the league). A club-side prediction model does not control the outcome, and the rules may change at the CBA expiration (unverified).
ASSUMPTION: [Blind spot] Dated snapshots are a precondition. Any backtest must freeze the data as of the decision day (projections, injury status, staff titles), or hindsight leaks into every candidate.
ASSUMPTION: [Blind spot] Testing many candidates and many specifications without a pre-registered baseline comparison produces false positives. Any claimed edge needs out-of-sample results against the simple rule.
ASSUMPTION: [Blind spot] Non-tender, QO, arbitration and posting all draw on one payroll and 40-man budget, so evaluating them separately misses interactions. Private Cubs practice is unknown, and public-data parity with sophisticated clubs is plausible for every candidate.

IDEA: Build a single pre-registered, dated-snapshot backtest harness for the offseason decisions (non-tender, QO, arbitration, posting). It would freeze public inputs as of each decision date, score each simple club baseline against a candidate model out of sample, and report n and interval width, so any candidate whose interval includes zero edge is dropped before software is built.
IDEA: Replace the coaching-ledger build with a persistence-first test: check on public data whether apparent coach effects in year T repeat in T+1 for coaches who moved clubs. Proceed to a hiring tool only if they persist beyond regression to the mean, and treat a null result as the useful output.
IDEA: Sharpen arbitration to settle-versus-hearing selection: estimate, from public filed-number gaps and past outcomes, the filing-gap threshold above which hearings favor the club. State the result as a decision table with explicit uncertainty rather than a point predictor.

ASSUMPTION: All evidence is UNVERIFIED and the facts map is empty, so every judgment below is a falsifiable critique drawn from general baseball knowledge, not a supported finding. CITE lines are omitted because no source supports any specific claim.

ASSUMPTION: Coaching-hire evaluation (1) The decision recurs every offseason but only a few hires per year, and the value per coach is unknown. UNKNOWN: detectable_coach_effect_size
ASSUMPTION: Coaching (2) Staff announcements are public, but assistant and minor-league tenure is patchy and inconsistently dated, so linking coaches to players at decision time may fail.
ASSUMPTION: Coaching (3) Coach moves between organizations are few, and most coaches touch few players, so a retrospective test has wide intervals. Outcomes are observable only as player stat changes, not as coach causation.
ASSUMPTION: Coaching (4,5) Hiring is driven by relationships, scheme fit and player buy-in that a panel cannot see. Rival clubs probably run private attribution with proprietary biomechanics and tracking data, so a public-data tool is likely behind.
ASSUMPTION: Coaching (6) It will look useful through regression to the mean, since players hired-for-after-a-bad-year improve anyway. Selection (teams acquire players they expect to improve), playing time, injuries and org infrastructure confound it. Post-hoc coach rankings that do not persist year over year would look good in-sample and fail out of sample.
UNKNOWN: persistence_of_coach_effects_year_over_year

ASSUMPTION: Non-tender (1) The decision recurs annually for roughly a handful of borderline players, so stakes are modest, bounded by the salary gap on a few roster spots. UNKNOWN: cubs_non_tender_candidates_2026
ASSUMPTION: Non-tender (2) Service time, projected arbitration salaries (public estimates exist) and the non-tender list are public, but the replacement pool is revealed only after the deadline. A forecast of who will be available must be made without hindsight, and that is the hard part.
ASSUMPTION: Non-tender (3) Roughly two decades of non-tender classes exist, but the CBA has changed salary and service rules, so older cases may not be comparable. Next-season output of non-tendered players is observable, but the output of the counterfactual tendered player is not, and survivorship in who signs where biases the comparison.
ASSUMPTION: Non-tender (4,5) It is actionable, since the club decides by the deadline. Clubs already use WAR-per-dollar thresholds, and public arbitration projection tools exist, so the marginal edge is likely small.
ASSUMPTION: Non-tender (6) A backtest looks good when it credits signed non-tendered players' production without netting out the many who flopped or were never signed, or when it uses the final arbitration salary instead of the projection known in November.

ASSUMPTION: Qualifying offers (1) The Cubs face the decision only for their own eligible free agents, which may be zero to a few per year. The stake is a one-year QO salary against a draft-pick change, so the value is moderate and lumpy. UNKNOWN: cubs_qo_eligible_players_2026
ASSUMPTION: Qualifying offers (2) Performance, age and the QO amount are public. Acceptance depends on private player preferences and agent strategy.
ASSUMPTION: Qualifying offers (3) The number of historical QOs is a few dozen per year at most, with an early period of nearly zero acceptances and a later period with some, so the pooled model is small and non-stationary. Acceptance is observable, but the counterfactual of not offering is not. UNKNOWN: historical_qo_acceptance_count_by_year
ASSUMPTION: Qualifying offers (4,5) It is actionable in a short window after the World Series. Clubs reason about this with simple market-versus-QO logic, and a sharper model probably adds little over an experienced executive.
ASSUMPTION: Qualifying offers (6) A high AUC in-sample may come from a few features (large AAV expectation means decline) that the baseline already uses. Rule changes to compensation across CBAs also confound the pooled history.

ASSUMPTION: NPB/KBO posting bids (1) Few relevant events per year, so recurrence is low, but the per-signing value can be large. Cubs interest in a given year is unknown. UNKNOWN: cubs_international_budget_2027
ASSUMPTION: NPB/KBO (2) Basic stats are public, but detailed pitch tracking is mostly proprietary or inconsistently published, so the translation tool may only have stats the baseline ratios already use. UNKNOWN: public_availability_of_npb_kbo_pitch_tracking
ASSUMPTION: NPB/KBO (3) The number of posted players with several MLB seasons is small, probably tens, split across hitters and pitchers and across ball and rule eras. A model with many parameters will overfit. Outcomes are observable but heterogeneous by role and injury. UNKNOWN: count_of_posted_players_with_mlb_outcomes
ASSUMPTION: NPB/KBO (4,5) Bids are actionable only in a short, rule-bound window and posting fees and caps depend on current agreements. Clubs with international scouts and data staff already model translation, and the price is set by multi-club competition, so the winner's curse may erase any accuracy edge.
ASSUMPTION: NPB/KBO (6) It looks useful through survivorship (only successes recalled), a few outlier stars driving fit, and comparing to the weakest ratio baseline instead of scouting-informed pricing.

ASSUMPTION: Postseason roster construction (1) It recurs only when the club qualifies, 1 to 4 times a year, so expected value is discounted by playoff probability. A marginal win may be worth more in October, but the number of slots that actually change outcomes is small. UNKNOWN: measured_win_probability_value_of_marginal_postseason_slot
ASSUMPTION: Postseason (2) Rosters, platoon and pitch-type splits are public, but injury status at the roster deadline is often incomplete or vague, which limits reconstruction of the true option set. UNKNOWN: public_injury_status_completeness_at_roster_deadline
ASSUMPTION: Postseason (3) Postseason rosters from many series exist league-wide, but the per-series sample is tiny and series outcomes are very noisy. A test would need to score recommendations by simulated expected win probability, and the simulation embeds the same assumptions it tests, so it is not an observed-outcome validation.
ASSUMPTION: Postseason (4,5) It is actionable and contenders already do this internally with staff judgment, so a public tool likely only matches.
ASSUMPTION: Postseason (6) It looks useful through hindsight-chosen anecdotes (a pinch runner who scored), unmeasurable gains of well under a percentage point of series win probability, and ignoring that managers concentrate innings on top pitchers whatever the 26th slot is. Note the candidate text supplied for this item lists only the decision, and the problem is narrower than its attached assumptions suggest.

ASSUMPTION: Arbitration filing (1) The Cubs file for each arbitration-eligible player every winter, which is several per year, with award differences per player in the range between filing numbers. Most cases settle, and hearings are rare for any one club.
ASSUMPTION: Arbitration (2) Hearing outcomes and filing figures are publicly reported, but the panel's reasoning is confidential, and settlement terms are inconsistently recorded. Comparable-player selection rules are set by the CBA, which may change after this offseason. UNKNOWN: post_2026_cba_arbitration_rules
ASSUMPTION: Arbitration (3) League-wide hearings are only a handful per year, so a predictor trained on hearings suffers from small samples and a selection effect: cases that reach hearing are those where the parties disagree, not a random draw. Outcome (win or loss against the two filed numbers) is observable. UNKNOWN: annual_hearing_count_sample_size
ASSUMPTION: Arbitration (4,5) Actionable by choosing the filing figure and deciding whether to settle. Clubs already employ specialized staff and outside counsel, and public salary-projection tools exist. A club-policy of avoiding hearings (a "file and trial" posture) also carries relationship costs a model does not capture.
ASSUMPTION: Arbitration (6) It looks useful through high accuracy that merely reflects the filing midpoint, hindsight about which stats panels reward, and treating the all-case outcome rate as if it applied to the cases a club would actually take to hearing.

ASSUMPTION: BLIND SPOT (a) All six are low-frequency, small-sample decisions. The set concentrates on offseason transactions and leaves out high-frequency decisions with larger samples, which the objective preferred.
ASSUMPTION: BLIND SPOT (b) Five of six depend on CBA rules that may change this offseason. The expiration timing is unverified. UNKNOWN: cba_expiration_date_verification
ASSUMPTION: BLIND SPOT (c) Every candidate's retrospective test measures outcomes of decisions made, not outcomes of the unchosen option. Counterfactuals are unobserved, and models validated on simulation inherit simulation bias.
ASSUMPTION: BLIND SPOT (d) No candidate states a baseline hit rate or dollar scale from supplied evidence, so the value-at-stake comparison is unsupported. UNKNOWN: cubs_private_models_and_practices
ASSUMPTION: BLIND SPOT (e) Software cost, adoption by decision-makers and the chance that clubs already run equivalent tools are not weighed against the possible edge. A null result is itself informative and cheap to get, so testing before building is the reasonable default.
IDEA: Sharpened replacement: one pooled "decision-quality audit" that, for non-tender, QO and arbitration decisions, uses only timestamped public data (projections and prices known on decision day) and reports the gap versus the simple baseline with bootstrap intervals. Build more only for the decision where the interval excludes zero by a margin larger than the dollar noise, and report a null for the others.

ASSUMPTION: [Coaching 1] The hire or retain decision recurs yearly, but only a handful of coaching slots turn over per club. Value per decision is plausibly large, yet no supplied evidence sizes it.
UNKNOWN: detectable_coach_effect_size
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching 2] Public inputs are Statcast, staff announcements and media guides. Assistant and minor-league role titles and dates are likely inconsistent, so the link from coach to player may be mislabeled.
UNKNOWN: public_coach_tenure_dataset_completeness
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching 3] The number of coach-movement events with enough players per coach is probably small, and the outcome (player change) is observable but very noisy. Intervals may be too wide to change any hiring decision.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching 4] Actionability is limited because the Cubs can hire only from available candidates, and coach quality is hard to separate from the hiring club's infrastructure.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching 5] Sophisticated clubs probably already track player development outcomes by staff internally. Public sources give mostly anecdote and press narrative, not rigorous attribution.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching 6] It would look useful through regression to the mean, survivorship (coaches get poached after good years), and teams acquiring players they already expect to improve. Pitch-mix changes may be driven by front-office strategy and not by the coach.

ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender 1] The decision recurs every November or December, but the Cubs' marginal cases (borderline tender candidates) are probably few per year. Stake per case is the gap between arbitration salary and replacement cost.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender 2] Public arbitration salary projections and the prior-year non-tender lists are public. The set of players other clubs will non-tender is not known when the Cubs decide, so any replacement-pool label built from the final list leaks hindsight unless it is forecast as of a dated snapshot.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender 3] Past decisions are many league-wide, and signing price and next-season output are observable. Players signed after non-tender are a selected sample, because injured or declining players are overrepresented.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender 4] Actionability is high and cheap to reverse. A club can tender, then trade or release, with partial cost, which weakens the need for a precise model.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender 5] Clubs already apply WAR-per-dollar thresholds with internal projections, and public arbitration projections are widely available.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender 6] It would look useful through hindsight-labeled replacement pools, and through backtests that count only the non-tendered players who succeeded. A comparison against a strawman threshold also flatters it.

ASSUMPTION: [QO 1] The decision recurs yearly only for players who are QO-eligible, so per-year count may be zero to a few. Stake is a compensation pick versus a one-year salary, and the pick's value depends on CBA terms I could not verify.

ASSUMPTION: [QO 2] Public data on age, WAR, and market depth is available at decision time. Agent intent and private willingness to accept are not public, and they dominate the acceptance outcome.
ASSUMPTION: [QO 3] Public history since the system began is only on the order of a hundred or so offers in total. That is too small for a calibrated model with many features, and each outcome is binary, which makes calibration weak.

ASSUMPTION: [QO 5] Clubs and public analysts already compare projected market AAV to the QO amount, so the mechanism is largely the baseline stated in the IDEA.
ASSUMPTION: [QO 6] It would look useful by overfitting a few dozen cases and by crediting hindsight on acceptance outcomes that were driven by market shocks.

ASSUMPTION: [Posting 3] The retrospective sample is small and heterogeneous across pitchers and hitters, ages, and ball and rule eras. MLB outcomes are observable but strongly censored by injury and playing time.
ASSUMPTION: [Posting 4] Actionability depends on posting fees, bid rules, and competition from other clubs. Any accuracy edge must also beat the winner's curse.
ASSUMPTION: [Posting 5] Clubs with international scouting and data feeds already run translation models. Public analysts publish translation factors, so the baseline "simple ratios" is probably weaker than actual club practice.
ASSUMPTION: [Posting 6] It would look useful through a handful of memorable hits and misses, and through fitting a model on survivors who were posted because they looked good. Narrow intervals from few cases would be false precision.

IDEA: Candidate 1, coaching-hire evaluation. Keep only as a null-result study, not a decision tool: a coach-movement panel with matched non-moving controls and a pre-registered test of year-over-year persistence of coach effects.

IDEA: Candidate 2, non-tender decisions. This is the strongest candidate: it recurs every year, the decision date is fixed, and tender decisions, projected salaries, and later signings are public, so a pooled backtest across all clubs is possible.

ASSUMPTION: Projected arbitration salaries are public only as third-party estimates, whose vintage as of the deadline must be preserved to avoid hindsight.
